prompt: Draw an off-grid cabin in the Highlands: a few solar panels, a small wind turbine, a battery bank and a diesel generator as backup, feeding lights, a fridge and a wood-pellet boiler's pump. Show that on a calm, cloudy evening the battery runs down and the generator starts, and that the fridge is never short.

Draw a district heat network: a gas CHP engine makes electricity and heat, a big thermal store tops up the network, and a hundred flats and a leisure centre draw heat. The CHP runs hardest in the morning peak, the store charges overnight and discharges at breakfast, and nobody goes cold.

Draw a house that harvests rainwater: the roof collects rain into an underground tank, a pump lifts it to the toilets and the garden, and mains water tops the tank up when it runs low. An afternoon storm should fill the tank; the toilets are never short.

Draw a hospital's power: mains through a breaker, a UPS battery, two diesel generators with a fuel tank, feeding theatres, wards and the chillers. Add a switch to trip the mains. With the mains on, the generators stay off; theatres are never short.

Draw a motorway EV charging hub: a limited grid connection, a battery that buffers it, and eight rapid chargers whose demand peaks at lunchtime and in the early evening. The battery charges overnight and covers the peaks, so the grid connection never goes over its limit.

Draw a dairy farm's biogas plant: slurry feeds an anaerobic digester, the gas goes to a gas holder and a generator, the generator's heat warms the digester and the milking parlour, and spare electricity is exported. Milking happens at 5am and 4pm.

Draw a small town's water supply: river intake, a treatment works, a pumped main up to a hilltop service reservoir, and the town below fed by gravity. Morning and evening demand peaks; the reservoir should drop during the day and recover overnight without ever running empty.

Draw a data centre whose waste heat warms a public swimming pool next door through a heat pump, with dry coolers dumping whatever heat the pool can't take. Show the pool getting most of its heat from the servers in the evening.

Draw a wind farm whose spare power runs an electrolyser making hydrogen into a storage tank, which a fuel cell turns back into electricity when the wind drops. The town it serves is never short, and the tank fills on the windy night.

Draw a home with an air-source heat pump, a hot water cylinder and underfloor heating, on a time-of-use tariff: the heat pump heats the cylinder cheaply overnight and the house in the morning and evening. The showers are never cold.

Draw a tidal lagoon power station: the sea fills the lagoon through sluices on the flood tide, and the turbines generate as it empties on the ebb, feeding the grid. Show two generating windows in a day.

Draw a primary school with rooftop solar, a battery and night-storage heaters: the panels cover the daytime load during lessons, the battery takes the surplus at lunch, and the storage heaters charge overnight off the grid.

Draw a P&ID of a cooling water loop: a pump draws from a cooling tower basin, pushes water through a plate heat exchanger that cools a process, and back up to the tower. A temperature transmitter on the return line feeds a temperature controller that throttles a control valve on the supply. Show the pump running all day and the valve opening further in the afternoon heat.

Draw a P&ID of a chlorine dosing skid: a day tank of hypochlorite, a metering pump, a non-return valve and an isolating valve into a town water main. A flow meter on the main tells a flow controller how hard to drive a control valve on the dosing line. Show the dose following the morning and evening demand peaks, and the day tank running down.

Draw a P&ID of a boiler feedwater system: make-up water comes in from off the sheet through a level control valve into a feedwater tank, a feed pump lifts it into a steam drum, and the drum's steam leaves off the sheet. A level transmitter and controller hold the tank level by working the make-up valve. Show the tank never running dry.

Draw a single-line diagram of a factory's electrical supply: an 11 kV intake, a transformer stepping down to 400 V, an incoming breaker onto the main LV board, and feeders with their own breakers to the production line, the compressors and the offices. Show the production line's load jumping when the shift starts at 6 and the transformer never overloading.

Draw a single-line diagram of a 5 MW solar farm: four PV arrays, each through its own inverter and breaker onto a collector busbar, then a step-up transformer and a breaker to the grid connection. Show the export peaking at midday and nothing exported at night.

Draw a single-line diagram of a hospital's supply: the utility feed through a transformer and breaker to the main board, a standby generator with its own breaker, and essential and non-essential feeders. During a grid outage from 14:00 to 16:00 the generator starts and carries the essential load, and the non-essential load is shed.

Draw a process flow diagram of a small brewery's hot side: a gas boiler heats water for the mash tun, the wort goes to a kettle to boil, then through a plate cooler into a fermenter, with the cooler's warm water going back to a hot liquor tank. Show the boiler working hardest during the morning boil and the hot liquor tank filling up afterwards.

Draw a process flow diagram of a water treatment works: raw water from a reservoir is pumped through a clarifier and sand filters into a clear water tank, which feeds the town. Show the clear water tank buffering the evening peak so the town is never short.

reference.xml in this folder is a P&ID exported as DEXPI from our plant design software. Turn it into a living P&ID saved as scene.json, keeping the plant's own tags, and give it an expect list that tells what the plant does over a day: product leaving the sheet, and the tank level moving.

Here is a flowsheet in SFILES 2.0 notation: (raw)(mix)<1(pp)(hex)(r)(dist)[{bout}(prod)]{tout}(splt)1(prod). Make it a living process flow diagram saved as scene.json, with an expect list saying product leaves from both the column's bottom and its overhead, and the feed pump carries everything that enters.

A rural street fed from one 230 V transformer at the end of a long overhead line: six houses along it, each span of cable losing a few volts at full load. Draw it as scene.json so the evening peak pushes the last house below 216 V while the first stays fine, with the voltages showing on the sheet and an expect list that says so.

Make a small Rube Goldberg machine as scene.json, built from real flows: a chain of at least four events where each one is set off by the one before (a tank filling trips a float, the float starts a pump, a timer follows, and so on), with an expect list that checks the chain really runs in order over the day.

Make scene.json: a greenhouse where a soil sensor, a pump and a vent run as a chain of events over a sunny day. Then save its storyboard as storyboard.png and the day as day.gif, and tell me what each panel shows.
